tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

# towtank-drag

Drag on smooth circular cylinders towed through the tank. 1in, 2in and
1.5in cylinders, 0.6 m submerged.

## Reproducing the results and paper

Everything (forces, Cd, figures, and `paper/paper.pdf`) is produced by the
Calkit pipeline defined in `calkit.yaml`:

```sh
calkit run
```

Stages: `process-runs` (raw -> `results/forces.csv`), `compute-cd`
(`results/cd.csv`, `results/summary.json`), `plot-cd` and `plot-timeseries`
(`figures/*.pdf`), `summary-to-latex` (values for the paper), and
`build-paper`. Scripts are in `scripts/`. Building the paper needs Docker.

## Processing (old, superseded by the pipeline above)

1. `python process.py` (change DATA path to wherever the raw data is)
2. `python process_b3.py` for the March data (new DAQ format)
3. run `analysis.ipynb` -> Cd vs Re plot in figures/

`plot_timeseries.py` makes the example trace figure.

Calibration files are in data/calibration. Run log is data/run_log.csv.

old_matlab/ is Jamie's original processing script, kept for reference.

environments:
  main:
    path: requirements.txt
    kind: uv-venv

    kind: docker

  stages:
    process-runs:
      kind: python-script
      script_path: scripts/process_runs.py
      environment: main
      description: Reduce each raw run to a mean drag force.
      inputs:
        - scripts/towtank.py
        - data/run_log.csv

      outputs:
        - path: results/forces.csv
          storage: git

      kind: python-script
      script_path: scripts/compute_cd.py
      environment: main
      description: Compute Cd, Re, and related parameters, and summarize.
      inputs:
        - scripts/towtank.py
        - data/run_log.csv
        - results/forces.csv
      outputs:
        - path: results/cd.csv
          storage: git
        - path: results/summary.json
          storage: git
    plot-cd:
      kind: python-script
      script_path: scripts/plot_cd.py
      environment: main
      description: Plot Cd versus Re for all cylinders.
      inputs:
        - scripts/plotstyle.py
        - results/cd.csv
      outputs:
        - path: figures/cd-vs-re.pdf
          storage: git
    plot-timeseries:
      kind: python-script
      script_path: scripts/plot_timeseries.py
      environment: main
      description: Plot force time series for a typical and the excluded runs.
      inputs:
        - scripts/plotstyle.py
        - scripts/towtank.py
        - results/cd.csv
        - data/raw
        - data/calibration
      outputs:
        - path: figures/force-timeseries.pdf
          storage: git

      inputs:

      outputs:
        - path: paper/generated-results.tex

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. - Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. """Compute drag coefficient, Reynolds number, and related parameters per run.

Writes a per-run table and a JSON summary whose keys are referenced from the
paper via the json-to-latex stage.
"""

import json

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from towtank import G, POST_WINDOW, STEADY_WINDOW, TARE_WINDOW

L_SUB = 0.60  # Submerged cylinder length (m)
TANK_WIDTH = 0.90  # m
TANK_DEPTH = 0.75  # m
# Runs whose load cell zero moved by more than this over the run are excluded
MAX_ZERO_DRIFT_N = 0.05

# Labels used in the run log, mapped to the key stems used in the paper
CYLINDERS = {"1in": "OneIn", "1.5in": "OnePointFiveIn", "2in": "TwoIn"}


def water_density(temp_c):
    """Density of air-free pure water (kg/m^3), Tanaka et al. (2001)."""
    a1, a2, a3, a4, a5 = -3.983035, 301.797, 522528.9, 69.34881, 999.974950
    t = temp_c
    return a5 * (1 - (t + a1) ** 2 * (t + a2) / (a3 * (t + a4)))


def water_viscosity(temp_c):
    """Dynamic viscosity of water (Pa s) from the Vogel equation."""
    return 2.414e-5 * 10 ** (247.8 / (temp_c + 273.15 - 140.0))


forces = pd.read_csv("results/forces.csv")
log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")
df = log.merge(forces, left_on="run_id", right_on="run")

d = df.diameter_mm / 1000
u = df.speed_m_s
df["rho"] = water_density(df.water_temp_c)
df["nu"] = water_viscosity(df.water_temp_c) / df.rho
df["Re"] = u * d / df.nu
df["Fr_D"] = u / np.sqrt(G * d)
df["Cd"] = df.F_mean_N / (0.5 * df.rho * u**2 * d * L_SUB)
# Cd with the fluctuating force std, to show the unsteadiness from shedding
df["Cd_std"] = df.F_std_N / (0.5 * df.rho * u**2 * d * L_SUB)
df["excluded"] = df.zero_drift_N.abs() > MAX_ZERO_DRIFT_N

cols = [
    "run_id", "date", "cylinder", "diameter_mm", "speed_m_s",
    "water_temp_c", "rho", "nu", "Re", "Fr_D", "F_mean_N", "F_std_N",
    "zero_drift_N", "Cd", "Cd_std", "excluded",
]
df[cols].to_csv("results/cd.csv", index=False)

good = df[~df.excluded]
excluded = df[df.excluded]
summary = {
    "NRuns": int(len(df)),
    "NRunsUsed": int(len(good)),
    "NRunsExcluded": int(len(excluded)),
    "ExcludedRuns": ", ".join(str(r) for r in excluded.run_id),
    "ExcludedZeroDrift": ", ".join(
        f"{x:.1f}" for x in excluded.zero_drift_N
    ),
    "MaxZeroDriftThreshold": MAX_ZERO_DRIFT_N,
    "MaxZeroDriftUsed": round(good.zero_drift_N.abs().max(), 3),
    "TareStart": TARE_WINDOW[0],
    "TareEnd": TARE_WINDOW[1],
    "SteadyStart": STEADY_WINDOW[0],
    "SteadyEnd": STEADY_WINDOW[1],
    "PostStart": POST_WINDOW[0],
    "PostEnd": POST_WINDOW[1],
    "SubmergedLength": L_SUB,
    "TankWidth": TANK_WIDTH,
    "TankDepth": TANK_DEPTH,
    "SpeedMin": float(df.speed_m_s.min()),
    "SpeedMax": float(df.speed_m_s.max()),
    "NSpeeds": int(df.speed_m_s.nunique()),
    "TempMin": float(df.water_temp_c.min()),
    "TempMax": float(df.water_temp_c.max()),
    "ReMin": int(round(good.Re.min(), -2)),
    "ReMax": int(round(good.Re.max(), -2)),
    "FrMin": round(good.Fr_D.min(), 2),
    "FrMax": round(good.Fr_D.max(), 2),
    "SensOld": round(df[df.date < "2026-03-10"].sens_V_per_N.iloc[0], 5),
    "SensNew": round(df[df.date >= "2026-03-10"].sens_V_per_N.iloc[0], 5),
    "CalResidMax": round(df.cal_resid_max_N.max(), 3),
    "CdMeanAll": round(good.Cd.mean(), 3),
    "CdStdAll": round(good.Cd.std(), 3),
    "CdMinAll": round(good.Cd.min(), 3),
    "CdMaxAll": round(good.Cd.max(), 3),
    "CdExcluded": ", ".join(f"{x:.2f}" for x in excluded.Cd),
    "CdFluctMax": round(good.Cd_std.max(), 2),
}
for label, stem in CYLINDERS.items():
    g = df[df.cylinder == label]
    gg = good[good.cylinder == label]
    dia = g.diameter_mm.iloc[0] / 1000
    summary[f"D{stem}"] = float(g.diameter_mm.iloc[0])
    summary[f"Date{stem}"] = g.date.iloc[0]
    summary[f"Temp{stem}"] = round(g.water_temp_c.mean(), 1)
    summary[f"N{stem}"] = int(len(gg))
    summary[f"CdMean{stem}"] = round(gg.Cd.mean(), 3)
    summary[f"CdStd{stem}"] = round(gg.Cd.std(), 3)
    summary[f"ReMin{stem}"] = int(round(gg.Re.min(), -2))
    summary[f"ReMax{stem}"] = int(round(gg.Re.max(), -2))
    summary[f"AspectRatio{stem}"] = round(L_SUB / dia, 1)
    # Width blockage D/W and frontal-area blockage D L / (W H), in percent
    summary[f"BlockageWidth{stem}"] = round(100 * dia / TANK_WIDTH, 1)
    summary[f"BlockageArea{stem}"] = round(
        100 * dia * L_SUB / (TANK_WIDTH * TANK_DEPTH), 1
    )

"""Reduce every raw run to a mean drag force.

Replaces process.py and process_b3.py: one code path for both DAQ formats,
with the sensitivity fitted from the calibration valid for each batch.

import pandas as pd

from towtank import (
    BATCHES,
    POST_WINDOW,
    STEADY_WINDOW,
    TARE_WINDOW,
    calibration,
    read_run,
    window,
)

log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")

rows = []
for _, r in log.iterrows():
    batch = r.date
    if batch not in BATCHES:
        raise ValueError(f"No batch config for {batch}")
    sens, cal_resid_N = calibration(batch)
    t, v = read_run(batch, r.run_id)
    tare = v[window(t, TARE_WINDOW)].mean()
    post = v[window(t, POST_WINDOW)].mean()
    force = (v - tare) / sens
    steady = force[window(t, STEADY_WINDOW)]
    rows.append(
        {
            "run": r.run_id,
            "sens_V_per_N": sens,
            "cal_resid_max_N": cal_resid_N,
            "F_mean_N": steady.mean(),
            "F_std_N": steady.std(),
            # Shift of the zero over the run; a large value means the
            # tare can't be trusted
            "zero_drift_N": (post - tare) / sens,
        }
    )

pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv("results/forces.csv", index=False)

"""Shared helpers for reading tow tank runs and converting them to force."""

import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Each test day, with its DAQ file format and the load cell calibration that
# was valid at the time (the load cell was remounted and recalibrated on
# 2026-03-10, see notes.md)
BATCHES = {
    "2025-10-14": {"fmt": "v2.1", "cal": "loadcell_2025-09.csv"},
    "2025-11-03": {"fmt": "v2.1", "cal": "loadcell_2025-09.csv"},
    "2026-03-12": {"fmt": "semicolon", "cal": "loadcell_2026-03.csv"},
}
RAW_DIR = "data/raw"
CAL_DIR = "data/calibration"
G = 9.81

# Time windows (s): load cell zero before the carriage starts, steady towing,
# and the zero after the carriage has stopped
TARE_WINDOW = (0.0, 1.0)
STEADY_WINDOW = (3.0, 8.0)
POST_WINDOW = (11.0, 12.0)


def run_path(batch, run):
    return os.path.join(RAW_DIR, batch, f"run_{run:03d}.csv")


def read_run(batch, run):
    """Return time (s) and load cell voltage (V) for one run."""
    fmt = BATCHES[batch]["fmt"]
    path = run_path(batch, run)
    if fmt == "v2.1":
        d = pd.read_csv(path, comment="#")
        return d.time_s.values, d.loadcell_V.values
    elif fmt == "semicolon":
        d = pd.read_csv(path, sep=";")
        return d.t.values, d.V.values
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown DAQ format {fmt}")


def calibration(batch):
    """Fit V = sens * F + offset to the static calibration for a batch.

    Returns sensitivity (V/N) and the maximum fit residual expressed in N.
    """
    cal = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(CAL_DIR, BATCHES[batch]["cal"]))
    force = cal.mass_g / 1000 * G
    sens, offset = np.polyfit(force, cal.voltage_V, 1)
    resid = cal.voltage_V - (sens * force + offset)
    return sens, np.abs(resid).max() / sens


def window(t, lo_hi):
    return (t >= lo_hi[0]) & (t < lo_hi[1])

bluff-body aerodynamics and hydrodynamics. Over the subcritical range of

constant~\citep{Wieselsberger1921,Roshko1961,Williamson1996,Zdravkovich1997}.
Measured values in practice also depend on blockage, aspect ratio, and end
conditions~\citep{WestApelt1982,Zdravkovich1997}.

$C = 140~\si{K}$.

518	from the Vogel equation $\mu = A\,10^{B/(T-C)}$ with
519	$A = 2.414\times10^{-5}~\si{Pa.s}$, $B = 247.8~\si{K}$, and
520	$C = 140~\si{K}$.
521	\todo[inline]{Cite a source for these Vogel constants, or switch to a standard
522	reference correlation such as IAPWS.}

524	\result[FrMin] to \result[FrMax].

535	\result[MaxZeroDriftUsed]~\si{N}.

Replaces process.py and process_b3.py: one code path for both DAQ formats,

import pandas as pd

from towtank import (
    BATCHES,
    POST_WINDOW,
    STEADY_WINDOW,
    TARE_WINDOW,
    calibration,
    read_run,
    window,
)

log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")

rows = []
for _, r in log.iterrows():
    batch = r.date
    if batch not in BATCHES:
        raise ValueError(f"No batch config for {batch}")
    sens, cal_resid_N = calibration(batch)
    t, v = read_run(batch, r.run_id)
    tare = v[window(t, TARE_WINDOW)].mean()
    post = v[window(t, POST_WINDOW)].mean()
    force = (v - tare) / sens
    steady = force[window(t, STEADY_WINDOW)]
    rows.append(

            "sens_V_per_N": sens,
            "cal_resid_max_N": cal_resid_N,
            "F_mean_N": steady.mean(),
            "F_std_N": steady.std(),
            # Shift of the zero over the run; a large value means the
            # tare can't be trusted
            "zero_drift_N": (post - tare) / sens,
        }
    )

"""Shared helpers for reading tow tank runs and converting them to force."""

import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Each test day, with its DAQ file format and the load cell calibration that
# was valid at the time (the load cell was remounted and recalibrated on
# 2026-03-10, see notes.md)
BATCHES = {
    "2025-10-14": {"fmt": "v2.1", "cal": "loadcell_2025-09.csv"},
    "2025-11-03": {"fmt": "v2.1", "cal": "loadcell_2025-09.csv"},
    "2026-03-12": {"fmt": "semicolon", "cal": "loadcell_2026-03.csv"},
}
RAW_DIR = "data/raw"
CAL_DIR = "data/calibration"
G = 9.81

# Time windows (s): load cell zero before the carriage starts, steady towing,
# and the zero after the carriage has stopped
TARE_WINDOW = (0.0, 1.0)
STEADY_WINDOW = (3.0, 8.0)
POST_WINDOW = (11.0, 12.0)


def run_path(batch, run):
    return os.path.join(RAW_DIR, batch, f"run_{run:03d}.csv")


def read_run(batch, run):
    """Return time (s) and load cell voltage (V) for one run."""
    fmt = BATCHES[batch]["fmt"]
    path = run_path(batch, run)
    if fmt == "v2.1":
        d = pd.read_csv(path, comment="#")
        return d.time_s.values, d.loadcell_V.values
    elif fmt == "semicolon":
        d = pd.read_csv(path, sep=";")
        return d.t.values, d.V.values
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown DAQ format {fmt}")


def calibration(batch):
    """Fit V = sens * F + offset to the static calibration for a batch.

    Returns sensitivity (V/N) and the maximum fit residual expressed in N.
    """
    cal = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(CAL_DIR, BATCHES[batch]["cal"]))
    force = cal.mass_g / 1000 * G
    sens, offset = np.polyfit(force, cal.voltage_V, 1)
    resid = cal.voltage_V - (sens * force + offset)
    return sens, np.abs(resid).max() / sens


def window(t, lo_hi):
    return (t >= lo_hi[0]) & (t < lo_hi[1])

the measured drag, so a correction~\citep[e.g.,][]{Maskell1963,WestApelt1982}
would lower $C_D$, more for the larger cylinders. The near-equality of the
uncorrected per-cylinder means therefore does not carry over automatically
to the corrected values.

The submerged aspect ratio ranges from \result[AspectRatioTwoIn] to
\result[AspectRatioOneIn]. A finite span with a free lower end generally
reduces the sectional drag relative to a two-dimensional
cylinder~\citep{Zdravkovich1997}. At the upper end the cylinder pierces the
free surface, and with $\Fr$ up to \result[FrMax] the surface deformation
and wave making at the higher speeds may contribute to the measured force.

# Response to reviewers

We thank the reviewers for their comments. The data reduction has been moved
from the original notebook into a single scripted pipeline, and every number
in the revised manuscript is now generated directly from it.

## Reviewer 1

**1. Reynolds numbers computed with the viscosity of water at 20 °C.**

The reviewer is correct. The previous version used ν = 1.004 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s
(20 °C) for every run. In the revision, ρ and ν are evaluated at each run's
measured water temperature (13.7–17.6 °C): density from Tanaka et al. (2001)
and dynamic viscosity from the Vogel equation (Sect. 3). Both Re_D and C_D
use these properties. Because the water was colder than 20 °C, the Reynolds
numbers are lower than before; the maximum is now 49,900 (previously about
55,700). The Fig. 1 caption also says that properties are evaluated at the
measured temperature.

**2. Run 17 (2 in. cylinder).**

We excluded run 17. We now also measure the load cell zero after each run and
exclude any run whose zero shifted by more than 0.05 N. Run 17 is the only run
that meets this criterion: its zero shifted by 4.2 N, and its force rose
steadily through the towing window. The paper describes the criterion and the
exclusion in Sect. 3 ("Run exclusion"), shows the run's force record in
Fig. 2 (bottom), and marks the run separately in Fig. 1. The abstract also
states the exclusion. For all retained runs the zero moved by at most
0.003 N. Without run 17, the 2 in. cylinder's mean C_D is 1.157 ± 0.034,
which agrees with the other two cylinders.

## Reviewer 2

**1. Range of Reynolds numbers in the abstract.**

The abstract now states that the diameter-based Reynolds numbers span 4,700
to 49,900, within the subcritical regime.
